#41562. Data-Driven Predictive Control for Autonomous Vehicle Racing under Varying Friction

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (283 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Data-Driven Predictive Control for Autonomous Vehicle Racing under Varying Friction

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (283 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21378v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DPC) predicts future outputs by combining recorded input-output trajectory data such that the combined trajectory approximately matches a measured initial trajectory and tracks a provided reference. This paper investigates to what extent and under which conditions DPC using data pooled across operating conditions retains the prediction accuracy of DPC using data from the current operating condition. In autonomous vehicle racing, the tire-road friction varies between racetrack sections and tire sets. If the initial trajectory and the recorded data originate from different frictions, prediction accuracy of DPC degrades. Ensuring the frictions match requires knowing the friction during recording and estimating the current friction explicitly. Instead, we pool data recorded at different frictions. We compare the prediction accuracy of DPC using data recorded under the current friction (matched), a different friction (mismatched) and data pooled from both frictions. We evaluate in simulation and small-scale vehicle experiments in the Cyber-Physical Mobility Lab (CPM Lab). Our results show that pooled data keep the multi-step root-mean-square prediction error within 1.5 times that of matched data, whereas mismatched data increase it by a factor of 2.2 to 3.4. To assess how this prediction accuracy carries over to control, we evaluate the tracking error from the raceline in closed loop. In simulation, DPC with pooled data tracks comparably to nonlinear model predictive control (13.7 cm versus 13.3 cm) and close to DPC with matched data in the CPM Lab, differing by 0.1 cm on the low-friction tires (1.6 cm versus 1.5 cm) and by 0.2 cm on the high-friction tires (0.9 cm versus 1.1 cm). DPC thus provides partial adaptation to varying friction, without a dedicated adaptation method.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2510.14289v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We revisit the Bohr-Sommerfeld atomic model to explore hydrogen-like ions of Uranium ($Z=92$), Oganesson ($Z=118$), and hypothetical superheavy elements beyond. Although superseded by the Dirac equation and modern quantum electrodynamics, the semiclassical approach offers a historically and pedagogically valuable perspective. Using the Sommerfeld fine structure formula and computer algebra methods, we demonstrate the appearance of self-intersecting orbits in super strong Coulomb fields, beginning with Oganesson and hypothetical elements up to $Z\le137$. These orbits can be classified by their `winding' numbers, providing a simple topological description of Coulomb field strength in this framework. Our results highlight a conceptual bridge between early quantum theory and modern superheavy element physics.

#41559. D\'ej\`a-Events: Multi-view 3D Geometry with Event Cameras via Sparsity-Aware Adaptive Gating

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (251 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

D\'ej\`a-Events: Multi-view 3D Geometry with Event Cameras via Sparsity-Aware Adaptive Gating

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (251 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21302v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Event cameras keep capturing structure where conventional cameras blur or saturate, which makes them attractive for 3D perception in fast or poorly lit scenes. Event datasets with dense 3D ground truth, however, are far smaller and less diverse than the image collections behind feed-forward 3D reconstruction models. We present D\'ej\`a-Events, an event-only model that predicts depth, camera pose and pointmaps from multiple views in a single forward pass. Rather than relying on scarce 3D labels, we distil it from D\'ej\`a View, a feed-forward RGB model that refines its tokens by repeatedly applying one shared transformer block. On paired RGB and event recordings, the event student learns to reproduce the frozen teacher's final tokens, which requires no depth or pose ground truth and trains only about 1% of its parameters. Because events are dense at edges and moving texture but nearly absent in textureless regions, we further introduce sparsity-aware adaptive gating, which adapts the shared block's gates to events and adjusts them per patch by event density, so that accuracy holds as refinement steps are added. Trained only on simulated data, D\'ej\`a-Events achieves the lowest pointmap error among the event-based methods we evaluate, on EventScape and zero-shot on the real MVSEC and DSEC datasets. On DSEC it halves the error of the strongest baseline (0.15 vs. 0.30 AbsRel) with about a tenth of its parameters. It also has the lowest depth error on EventScape and DSEC and the lowest trajectory error on EventScape.

From Rotations to Unitaries: Reversible Quantum Processes and the Emergence of the $SU(2)-SO(3)$ Homomorphism

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (132 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

Sources indicate that arXiv:2508.16691v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present an operational reconstruction of the well-known two-to-one homomorphism between the groups $SU(2)$ and $SO(3)$, grounded in the physical description of quantum state preparation and evolution. Starting from the connection between vectors in three-dimensional physical space and quantum states of two-level systems, we investigate how reversible transformations-modeled as completely positive and trace-preserving maps-give rise to a correspondence between spatial rotations and unitary operations. Our approach reveals how this group-theoretic structure naturally emerges from physical constraints, particularly the preservation of purity and reversibility in quantum processes. Beyond its theoretical relevance, the construction offers a pedagogically accessible framework for introducing core ideas in quantum mechanics and symmetry groups, making the abstract correspondence between $SU(2)$ and $SO(3)$ tangible through experimentally meaningful procedures.

Industry News: MVSTF: Multi-View Spatio-Temporal Fusion for LiDAR-Based Moving Object Segmentation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (212 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.20872v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autonomous mobile robots confront significant chal lenges in recognizing the motion properties of objects in dy namic environments. However, existing methods are hindered by limitations such as boundary ambiguity, occlusion, viewpoint constraints, and training complexity. In this paper, we propose an innovative end-to-end Multi-View Spatio-Temporal Fusion network, named MVSTF, which utilizes sequential point clouds to generate multi-view images and feature differences, and designs a multi-branch network to extract spatio-temporal and dimen sional features in parallel, and realizes high-precision moving object segmentation. First, sequential point clouds are utilized to generate multi-view images and feature differences. Then, an end-to-end multi-branch network including Dual Down-sampling Blocks (DDB), Spatial Attention Blocks (SAB), Multi-Kernel Convolutional Neural Network blocks (MKCNN), Dual Feature Fusion Blocks (DFFB), and the Point Fusion (PF) module, is designed to extract motion features from feature differences and geometric and semantic features from multi-view images. Finally, an auxiliary semantic head is introduced to further improve the algorithm's robustness and the model's interpretability. This work is validated on the SemanticKITTI and KITTI-Road bench marks, achieving state-of-the-art results on the SemanticKITTI MOS validation set and the KITTI-Road validation set, and competitive results on the hidden SemanticKITTI-MOS test set. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhouJJ111/MVSTF.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Geometric encoding of turbulence for end-to-end quantum simulation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (167 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2508.05346v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Simulating multiscale turbulence in engineering remains challenging. Any quantum advantage for such simulations requires efficient initial-state preparation. Yet exact loading of an arbitrary classical snapshot requires exponential quantum resources. We introduce "turbuloscope", a physics-informed geometric method that generates statistically representative turbulent initial states in a gate-based register from a parameterized Pauli-spinor multiscale distribution. Scale invariance renders conditional rotations approximately affine in Gray-code space, enabling linear-depth, ancilla-free preparation. The generalized Madelung transform and Hopf fibration map the encoded Pauli spinor to fluid observables and vortex tubes. The qubit count scales logarithmically with the Reynolds number, yielding an exponential reduction in preparation overhead relative to full-grid classical spectral synthesis. We classically emulate a 30-qubit preparation circuit and generate a turbulent field over one billion grid points at a scale-inferred Reynolds number of 35,000, exhibiting Kolmogorov's five-thirds energy spectrum, tangled vortex tubes, and intermittency. This method provides scalable initial states for quantum simulation of turbulence and multiscale systems.

📖 Baca

Entanglement preservation and Clauser-Horne nonlocality in electromagnetically induced transparency quantum memories

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (193 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2507.15453v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Understanding how decoherence-induced loss affects entanglement and nonlocal correlations in quantum memories is notable for quantum information science. Here we develop a quantitative description of photonic quantum states retrieved from electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT) memories in a ground-state-decoherence-limited regime. Using the dark-state-polariton formalism, we derive the attenuation factor of the retrieved probe mode from the EIT dynamics. This attenuation depends on the coupling field and ground-state coherence decay and is not introduced as an independent phenomenological loss parameter. Within a specified quantum-limited pure-loss model, we use this attenuation to obtain the reduced photonic density operator. We show that, in the symmetric case, the complete retrieved state of an initially path-entangled single photon remains entangled for any nonzero storage efficiency, despite acquiring a vacuum component. In contrast, violation of the unconditional Clauser-Horne inequality under displaced on/off detection without post-selection requires an intrinsic efficiency above 89.7%. We further derive the retrieved N-qubit photonic density operator for multiple independently operating EIT memories. These results establish a quantitative connection between EIT memory dynamics, retrieved quantum states, and operational nonlocality benchmarks under explicit channel assumptions.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (153 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Correspondence-Free Camera Pose Estimation by Matching Moments

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (153 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.20797v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The blind perspective-$n$-point (PnP) problem is to estimate the pose of a calibrated camera from 2D and 3D point sets with unknown correspondences. We show that, for complete, noiseless observations, fourteen permutation-invariant image moments up to order four identify a fixed camera pose for almost every 3D point set containing at least twenty points. Our learning-free method, MomentPnP, matches these moments between the observed 2D points and the projected 3D points to initialize a camera pose without correspondences and refines the pose and correspondence weights using expectation--maximization. Across the test sets of three benchmarks, our method reduces median rotation error by $5$--$170\times$ relative to the best learned baseline, both with and without outliers. We recover accurate poses even with as many outliers as inliers. On dense ETH3D scans, pose accuracy improves as the point sets grow, even as individual correspondences become harder to resolve.

#41540. TRR: A Thermal Interaction Engine for Robot Simulation and RGBT Data Generation

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (248 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

TRR: A Thermal Interaction Engine for Robot Simulation and RGBT Data Generation

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (248 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.20792v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A robot's actions change the thermal conditions of its next interaction: heat retained after release, carried with objects or stored beneath the surface can change a later contact's outcome despite similar current temperatures. Training trajectories must capture how these effects connect earlier actions to later observations and task outcomes. We present TRR, a \emph{Thermal Robot Renderer} that attaches spatial and depth-resolved thermal state to both contact partners, updates local heat exchange through contact, transport and separation, and generates synchronized RGB--thermal (RGBT) observations and event-local task checks on one execution clock. Controlled interventions show why retained heat, spatial transport and internal storage matter for subsequent contact outcomes. From the same state, TRR produces a paired six-task benchmark of 2,224 static--dynamic pairs, that is, 4,448 trajectories with synchronized dual-view observations, states and actions. Visible thermal history raises safe contact-site selection from 75.0\% to 91.7\% on a dedicated learning corpus, and training on dynamic histories raises simulated transfer completion by 50 percentage points under a new heating procedure with shared feedback execution. We demonstrate RGBT observation adapters on MuJoCo and Isaac Sim, report an engineering inventory of ten prepared robot configurations and six demonstrated camera viewpoints, and describe a developer workflow that carries an existing robot scene to exported RGBT records. The benchmark, the workflow and the platform resources described in Section 6 form the first items of a planned public release. Demonstrations and resource updates are available on the project page.

#41537. Breaking: Quantum Advantage in Storage and Retrieval of Isometry Channels

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (253 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Quantum Advantage in Storage and Retrieval of Isometry Channels

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (253 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2507.10784v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Storage and retrieval refer to the task of encoding an unknown quantum channel $\Lambda$ into a quantum state, known as the program state, such that the channel can later be retrieved. There are two strategies for this task: classical and quantum strategies. The classical strategy uses multiple queries to $\Lambda$ to estimate $\Lambda$ and retrieves the channel based on the estimate represented in classical bits. The classical strategy turns out to offer the optimal performance for the storage and retrieval of unitary channels. In this work, we analyze the asymptotic performance of the classical and quantum strategies for the storage and retrieval of isometry channels. We show that the optimal fidelity for isometry estimation is given by $F = 1-{d(D-d)\over n} + O(n^{-4/3})$, where $d$ and $D$ denote the input and output dimensions of the isometry, and $n$ is the number of queries. This result indicates that, unlike in the case of unitary channels, the classical strategy is suboptimal for the storage and retrieval of isometry channels, which requires $n = \Theta(\epsilon^{-1})$ to achieve the diamond-norm error $\epsilon$. We propose a more efficient quantum strategy based on port-based teleportation, which stores the isometry channel in a program state using only $n = \Theta(1/\sqrt{\epsilon})$ queries, achieving a quadratic improvement over the classical strategy. As an application, we extend our approach to general quantum channels, achieving improved program cost compared to prior results by Gschwendtner, Bluhm, and Winter [Quantum \textbf{5}, 488 (2021)].

#41525. A Diamond Quantum Oscilloscope

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (189 w)

A Diamond Quantum Oscilloscope

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (189 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2105.06037v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Quantum-enhanced metrology has achieved remarkable precision in parameter estimation, but extending these advantages to continuous time-dependent fields (waveform sensing) remains a formidable challenge due to the infinite-dimensional nature of the signal. Here, we report the first experimental realization of a room-temperature solid-state quantum oscilloscope based on a sequential quantum difference amplification strategy. Within a zero-order-hold reconstruction framework, our method completely bypasses the need for massive entanglement. Crucially, we demonstrate that the overall waveform reconstruction error unequivocally follows the theoretically predicted Heisenberg scaling of \(O(N^{-1/2})\), decisively surpassing the classical \(O(N^{-1/3})\) limit. This transformative precision requires approximately 30-fold fewer quantum resources than conventional methods to achieve the same waveform error. Furthermore, we demonstrate the reconstruction of a multicomponent waveform and distinctly resolve weak high-frequency components that are entirely drowned in the shot noise of classical sampling. These results transition quantum metrology from parameter estimation into a practical instrument, establishing a genuine quantum advantage in continuous waveform reconstruction and paving the way for critical applications such as nanoscale nuclear magnetic resonance imaging, where detecting extremely weak signals is crucial for resolving molecular structures.

STA: A Split Temporal Adversary Method for Evaluating Robustness of Multimodal RL-based Driving Policies

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (250 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.20765v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning (MRL) offers a promising paradigm for autonomous driving by jointly leveraging complementary sensor observations to learn effective decision-making policies. However, its effectiveness critically depends on temporal alignment across modalities, making temporal inconsistency a fundamental vulnerability. Even subtle misalignment or latency can corrupt fused representations and ultimately lead to decision failures. Existing studies have explored adversarial attacks to induce cross-modal temporal inconsistencies, thereby enabling systematic evaluation of the temporal robustness of MRL policies. However, existing methods remain limited in generality, realism, and adaptivity. To address these limitations, we propose the Split Temporal Adversary (STA), which formulates multimodal temporal attacks as a unified decision process that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection under realistic policy-aware and budget-constrained settings. STA includes two mechanisms: a) a unified multimodal temporal perturbation mechanism that delays observations via historical states, removing the need for modality-specific noise; b) a split multimodal adversarial decision mechanism that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection through adaptive optimization while leveraging the victim policy's clean actions to identify sensitive decision patterns. We provide a theoretical analysis of the induced distribution shift and a modality selection principle. Experiments in the CARLA simulator show that STA more than doubles the collision rate of the strongest baseline against PPO while using 17.8\% fewer attack attempts, and that it generalizes to a VLM-based driving policy. These results reveal temporal consistency as a critical vulnerability, highlighting temporal robustness as essential for safe autonomous driving.

Instructions Before Actions: Prospective and Retrospective Language Supervision for Driving Vision-Language-Action Data

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (198 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.20631v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Driving vision-language-action (VLA) models can accept navigation instructions, yet predicting a driver's trajectory does not establish that a model follows the instruction. We study how driving-language supervision is collected and evaluated, distinguishing prospective instructions issued before an action from retrospective labels written after observing it. We develop ADVLAT-Engine to synchronize spoken instructions, road-scene video, and vehicle trajectories, and compare three navigation apps on 48 replayed routes. On 87 maneuvers confirmed by both Google Maps and a passenger, the passenger uses more scene-dependent language. We evaluate four open driving VLAs before and after fine-tuning on prospective navigation-app drives. Fine-tuning reduces passenger-drive trajectory error by 23-59%, but instruction effects remain inconsistent. At real intersections, counterfactual instructions reveal stronger responsiveness: fine-tuned Alpamayo~2 Super gains 31 and 18 accuracy points at 15 and 5~m, while Qwen-Drive follows alternative maneuvers more reliably with a discrete command than with a sentence. We additionally collected retrospective annotations from four people for the driving recordings and describe controlled comparisons of annotation content, timing, and downstream learning; those analyses are pending. Our findings separate maneuver prediction from instruction-following and establish a framework for comparing prospective and retrospective supervision.

#41517. Breaking: VoxSAOR: Semantic-Aware Occupancy Robustification via Aleatoric Uncertainty Modeling

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (224 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: VoxSAOR: Semantic-Aware Occupancy Robustification via Aleatoric Uncertainty Modeling

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (224 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.20507v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-based 3D occupancy prediction provides a dense semantic representation of scenes for autonomous driving and embodied perception, yet remains vulnerable to occlusion, depth ambiguity, and projection errors that induce spatially varying reliability in voxel features. Existing methods typically map voxel representations to semantic predictions without explicitly modeling such observation-induced feature variations. To address this limitation, we propose VoxSAOR, a semantic-aware occupancy robustification framework that models aleatoric uncertainty through feature-space proxies. It first quantifies Local Semantic Consistency (LSC) to derive a voxel-wise structural stability prior and uses cross-view semantic consensus to filter unreliable semantic correspondences. Within each semantic category, spatially matched stable and ambiguous voxels form stable-to-ambiguous feature transitions, which are modeled by a class-conditional diagonal Gaussian distribution, capturing both feature displacement and dispersion. Guided by these proxy distributions, Aleatoric Regime Ensemble Learning (AREL) trains independently parameterized prediction heads using feature perturbations at progressively increasing scales, with perturbation strength modulated by structural reliability. At inference, proxy modeling and sampling are disabled, and all heads process the same observed features; their output probabilities are then averaged to produce a deterministic consensus prediction without requiring sampling. Experiments across multiple datasets and occupancy backbones demonstrate the effectiveness of VoxSAOR in improving semantic occupancy prediction, long-tail recognition, and predictive calibration. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/MengfeiD/VoxSAOR.

Spin-Polarized Transport Tomography of a Quantum-Dot Spin Qubit via Ferromagnetic Leads

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (194 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2101.10821v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose a theoretical protocol for reconstructing the density matrix of a single-electron spin qubit using spin-polarized transport. The system consists of a quantum dot coupled to ferromagnetic reservoirs and subject to a magnetic field lying in the $xy$ plane of the Bloch sphere. Spin-dependent tunneling events measured along the $x\pm$, $y\pm$, and $z\pm$ quantization axes give rise to probability distributions that encode the quantum state of the qubit. The open-system dynamics are described using a Lindblad master equation, which captures the time evolution of the spin under continuous coupling to the reservoirs. By counting tunneling events for four different magnetic alignments, we formulate a scheme for reconstructing the full density matrix of the qubit. The resulting simulation data are analyzed using Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) as a supervised machine-learning post-processing tool to reconstruct smooth time-dependent density-matrix elements from the measured probability distributions. The proposed model enables complete access to the open-system density matrix, including both population probabilities and relative phase information. Successful state reconstruction demonstrates the validity and robustness of the approach, highlighting its applicability to experimentally accessible spin-transport platforms.

Quantum differential interference contrast microscope

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (195 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.22579v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Optical sensing and imaging of transparent unstained biological and material specimen makes use of optical interference to translate phase shifts into intensity measurements, that are readily available in the optical domain. This is the case of Differential Interference Contrast (DIC) microscopes. However, environmental disturbances such as acoustic vibrations, air currents, temperature shifts, and mechanical drifts cause random phase noise that degrades the precision attainable in the estimation of the unknown phase shift. Although there are tools to compensate for these random phase drifts, such using common path interference techniques or phase stabilization systems, these are not always an option and its introduction is generally at the expense of device simplicity and robustness. Here we introduce a quantum version of Differential Interference Contrast microscopy (qDIC), that makes use of quantum interference for polarization analysis. When compared with standard schemes that make use of coherent light, our approach reveals that the transfer of classical DIC microscopy into the quantum domain offers a route towards quantum-enhanced resilience to environmental disturbances, allowing the enhancement of phase sensitivity without sacrificing the simplicity and robustness of the optical setup.

Maximum consensus seeks one transformation that aligns as many matches as possible, while maximum clique selects matches through pairwise distance tests. Maximum clique is often used as a substitute for or an approximation to maximum consensus, with empirical evidence suggesting a close relationship. We show that, at any fixed positive tolerance, a maximum clique can have arbitrarily large alignment error and be arbitrarily larger than a maximum consensus set. When rotation is fixed, we derive sharp error bounds and tests that exactly characterize maximum consensus for the translation subproblem. We also study group-$k$ consistency, which uses consistency of groups of $k$ matches, and determine the smallest group sizes that guarantee alignment error bounds independent of point cloud scale and geometry. These are $d+1$ for rotations and translations and $d+2$ when reflections are allowed, in dimensions $d\ge2$. Finally, our experiments on nearly 8,000 registration examples quantify the frequency of these limitations in practice and show how the derived bounds can be used to check whether a subset of matches can be aligned within a point tolerance.

arXiv:2611.18467v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A diffusion equation can be rewritten as a transport equation driven by the score function of the evolving density. Conventional probability-flow formulations, which move particles deterministically with this score-driven velocity, typically conserve total mass. In this work, we develop a Lagrangian method for reaction-diffusion equations in which each particle carries a position and a physical weight. The characteristic ODEs incorporate source terms into the evolution of the log-density and its gradient, while particle weights track changes in mass. We combine this representation with a learned velocity field and weighted particle training to approximate these dynamics. For non-increasing reaction rates, a relative-entropy inequality supports the mass-normalized self-consistency residual as the training objective. This objective can control the error of the induced density when the growth rate is bounded. The algorithm divides the time interval into short windows. In each window, a frozen velocity generates the particle data for a regression of the network velocity. We draw the particles from period-adapted initial sampling distributions and weight them in the loss partly by their predicted future mass, because the reaction can make regions with little initial mass important later. We numerically investigate the method on the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) equation with a linear source term, Fisher-KPP equations, and Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao gradient flows.

arXiv:2607.24744v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multimodal foundation models learned to see and to speak by consuming the whole internet. Embodied agents admit no such shortcut, since they require data that couple observations with physical states and actions. These signals can be provided, to varying degrees, by multiple data sources. In this work, we organize the embodied data ecosystem as a "pyramid'' spanning five complementary sources: real-robot data, UMI-style data, egocentric and exocentric data, simulation data, and general vision-language data. We organize the pyramid around the tension between scalability and robot alignment, and further characterize each source in terms of data quality, diversity, reusability, and physical fidelity. We then analyze recent embodied foundation models through the lens of data recipes, examining how different sources are selected, aligned, and mixed during pretraining. For embodied brain models, vision-language-action models, and world-action models alike, we relate data composition to capabilities in perception, reasoning, planning, action generation, and world prediction. To facilitate community use, we additionally consolidate over 10,000 hours of trajectories from widely used robot datasets into a unified LeRobot format, with transparent frame-level quality annotations for filtering. We close by discussing six open challenges: building large-scale tactile datasets, collecting failure and recovery data, developing scalable data-collection pipelines, aligning actions across embodiments, leveraging egocentric data for dexterous manipulation, and designing principled data recipes for robot learning. We hope this work lays the foundation for the design of next-generation embodied systems.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2607.05598v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Novel View Synthesis (NVS) methods, such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), rely on the assumption of clean, multi-view consistent, posed input images. Real-world captures can violate this assumption due to \textbf{screen-space artifacts}---static occlusions fixed to the 2D image plane rather than to the 3D world. Common examples include physical sensor defects, environmental obstructions (such as rain or mud on the lens enclosure), capture obstructions (such as a thumb over the camera sensor or a dashboard visible in dashcam footage), and digital overlays (such as watermarks or UI elements). When present, they are erroneously baked into the 3D geometry as ``floaters'' or near-camera artifacts, degrading the quality of novel-view rendering. In this work, we propose \textit{SSA-3DGS}, an unsupervised framework that jointly optimizes a 3D scene and a learnable 2D overlay to recover a clean 3D scene and the corrupting artifacts. By exploiting geometric consensus across views, our method effectively disentangles static artifacts from the 3D scene geometry without supervision or manual input. Across diverse synthetic corruptions and a self-captured real-world dataset, SSA-3DGS improves reconstruction fidelity by up to ${\sim}8$~dB PSNR over 3DGS trained on the same corrupted inputs, while faithfully preserving the corrupting artifact.

At a defocus of about 25 $\mu$m, a crossed laser phase plate (XLPP) acts as the $\pi/2$ element, and APEX of a periodic specimen cell comes close to CTEM with the same plate. Trained on a medical corpus, our sparse codes improve in-domain retrieval over the original embeddings, and lose less out-of-domain performance than their dense counterparts, especially when the target corpus is distant from the training one. Importantly, our experiments show that the method yields interpretable features whose semantic content can be inferred from the queries and documents that activate them most strongly. The interpretation of these features sheds light on why a particular document was retrieved, and transfers beyond the training distribution.

With nothing tuned on test blocks, a 46,000-parameter detector gated by a contrast cue finds 10.4% of people against 5.7% for the same network applied everywhere. A standard detector, YOLO11n, trained under the same folds finds 54.5% at a similar false-alarm rate for about eleven times the arithmetic, and on our 4K field footage at 117 m has a walking person among its top 16 detections in up to 92% of frames against 74% for our board. Run alone, YOLO11n's thresholds set at one location overshot their false-alarm target 1.7 to 3.4 times at new locations, and its best configuration at altitude cost 4 to 24 standard passes per frame. Re-scoring its 16 best crops (154 KB per frame) with an 842,000-parameter ground model, thresholds frozen on a validation location, raised recall from 44.9% to 53.7% against the same 16 crops with YOLO's own scores; in a post hoc paired analysis over 15 test locations the gain was +8.8 points [+2.4, +12.5]. Pooled false detections fell from 0.86 to 0.64 per frame, but that paired change was not distinguishable from zero. Coverage of a still person in earth tones was very low for both detectors in the clips we flew.

To address the issue, we introduce an extension of the Ganeshan-Pixley-Das Sarma model with both asymmetric hopping and complex onsite potential, thereby incorporating a broad range of non-Hermitian quasiperiodic chains. According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.16246v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models drive the robot directly from camera views, yet a VLA alone shows three typical failures. It walks past the goal, stops before reaching it, and rarely recovers after going off track. Pairing a VLA with a large language model (LLM) planner fixes these failures, but queries the LLM throughout every episode, adding token costs and latency. We introduce Harness-to-Executor (H2E), a task-level distillation method that pairs an LLM planner and a frozen VLA as a heterogeneous training agent, keeps only sessions that reach the goal, and then trains a VLA alone on them so no LLM is used at test time. In these sessions, the planner gives sub-instructions and moves the robot with its own tools, detours are common, and the planner decides when to stop. H2E therefore labels every motion as a VLA action for the original task, whoever made it. It masks the loss on steps moving away from the goal and assigns end labels to states near it, so the VLA learns where the task ends. H2E sets a new state of the art on REVERIE-CE and NavRAG-CE. It raises an 8B VLA's success rate by 15.6% and 11.1% respectively, surpassing a method trained on 10M samples. The distilled VLA exceeds its agent on unseen episodes with zero LLM tokens and runs 3.7 times faster.

arXiv:2611.10357v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A generative recommender names each candidate with a short token sequence, a Semantic ID, and recommends by generating those tokens. Some generative recommenders, including the Uber Eats search engine we are building, write a whole results page, stores with their menu items, in one decoding pass. Every Semantic ID on such a page must name a real store or item that is eligible for the search, such as a store that delivers to the user's location, and that is not already on the page. Each item must also belong to the store above it. A trie over the catalog keeps identifiers real, but eligibility and repetition change with every request and token, and the grammar-constrained decoder we tried could not enforce these changing rules exactly and quickly. We call this constraint LEGIT, for live eligibility gating over identifier tries. Numbering trie leaves depth first turns each rule into a range lookup over one store trie and one item trie, and every generated page passes an independent catalog check. On one NVIDIA B200 GPU with one or two requests per decode step, a direct implementation that walks the trie on the GPU makes each token about 5 times as slow as unconstrained decoding. Across 36 implementations, hardware counters and ablations are consistent with kernel launches and CPU-GPU waits as the source of this slowdown. Our fastest implementation walks the trie on the CPU while the GPU runs the model, needs no custom kernel, and cuts time per output token by 65.9 percent against the direct GPU implementation, to about 1.7 times the unconstrained cost. This implementation is also the fastest on a page layout that puts each item before its store.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (259 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2611.20011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged in autonomous driving with the promise of strong generalization to long-tail scenarios. Although these models achieve state-of-the-art results on autonomous driving benchmarks, most existing benchmarks are dominated by nominal scenarios and therefore cannot test this promise. To test one such long-tail capability that is critical for safety, we introduce ReactBench-AD, a benchmark that measures how driving models react to objects that appear in the ego vehicle's path. Built on real NAVSIM and PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles scenes, ReactBench-AD composites a crossing pedestrian, a standing pedestrian, or a stationary car consistently across all camera views and history frames. Each edited scene thus forms an exact, pixel-level counterfactual pair with its original, which allows us to isolate the causal effect of the inserted object on the predicted trajectory. Evaluating four VLAs and two WAMs, we find that they react weakly, often barely at all. Finally, we test how easily one of the evaluated VLAs, ReCogDrive, can be taught to brake hard for imminent hazards: a short fine-tuning stage on edited scenes substantially improves its reactions, with the learned behavior generalizing to unseen objects and fully real scenes, at minimal cost to nominal driving. These results call into question the out-of-the-box long-tail capabilities of these models, but suggest that they can be a strong foundation for acquiring them with little additional training, highlighting the value of real or synthetic data that demonstrates the long-tail behaviors nominal datasets rarely contain. Code and data will be made publicly available.

Frame-active-state simulators isolate non-stabilizer information in a dense active-state vector, yet dense-state processing remains exponential in the active width. This paper presents MASQ, an exact measurement-adaptive sampler for near-Clifford QEC circuits based on selective materialization of non-Clifford rotations. Stabilizer-assisted elimination further removes rotations certified to be invisible to all future measurements. We find that a common result in this setting, that untrained or locally trained networks rival or beat backpropagation at early visual cortex, depends on the resolution at which networks are evaluated. In representational similarity analysis (RSA) against human V1, the gap between an untrained and a backprop-trained network grows monotonically from $-0.001$ (95% CI $[-0.011, 0.009]$) at the 32 px training resolution to $+0.030$ $[0.018, 0.042]$ at 224 px (six resolutions, 5 seeds; per-subject RSA on cross-run stimulus pairs). The growth reproduces for three further learning rules, directionally in single-seed macaque electrophysiology, along training, and for an ImageNet ResNet-50 and a Swin-Tiny transformer, which also align best at low resolution although trained at 224 px. Gabor and pixel structure, the normalization state of the untrained baseline, and a global brightness statistic do not account for it. Against a criterion fixed before the analysis, limiting image content to 32 px while the input still grows does not shrink the V1 gap ($+0.035$ $[0.023, 0.046]$ vs. $+0.030$ at 224 px; ratio 1.14 $[1.03, 1.34]$): it arises once the input exceeds the training resolution, through a decline of backprop. A single luminance value per image reaches rho= 0.054 against V1, matching the untrained network (0.053), which bounds what RSA on globally pooled features can resolve at V1 in this dataset. The one learning effect that holds across resolution is backprop above untrained at LOC. Comparisons of learning rules or architectures at early visual cortex need to control, and report, the evaluation resolution.

#41458. The Flip Test: Video World Models Fail to Learn the World State

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

The Flip Test: Video World Models Fail to Learn the World State

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (271 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.19822v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Video world models promise to predict the future of a scene from its present. Do current models keep this promise? We probe this question counterfactually. When a small change to the present flips the future, such as a box resting a few millimeters before or past a table edge, a model that tracks the state of the world must flip its prediction too. We build FlipTest, a three-level hierarchy of increasingly strict tests over 1,680 initial frames from 10 simulated and 15 real-world tasks. At the base, visual minimal pairs, two nearly identical frames whose true futures differ, test whether predictions change across the boundary; matched controls go further and test whether they change only where the future does; and dense sweeps, the strictest level, locate exactly where they change. All 11 video world models we evaluate fall short. The best averages 18.3% pair accuracy over real and simulated scenes, below the 25% of random guessing. Models flip as often on steps that leave the future unchanged as on steps that change it, and their response stays flat across the sweeps. On the same frames, a vision-language model is selective and traces a near S-shaped curve near the boundary, and a coding agent that measures the image comes close to the true boundary. This implies that the deciding information is in the frame, and video models just miss it. We therefore urge the community to rethink world modeling as pure video prediction. Next-frame prediction must do more than draw plausible pixels; it must also identify the causal states that control future dynamics.

In this study, we investigate the equilibrium electrostatics of BDD/nitrogen-doped diamond junctions using self-consistent Poisson-Fermi calculations. The results reveal two distinct electrostatic length scales in the nitrogen-doped substrate: a near-interface region of ionized donors that produces dominant band bending and determines the NV$^{0/-}$ charge-state boundary, and a much longer screening tail associated with weak donor ionization in the neutral bulk. The resulting NV$^-$ depletion depth depends strongly on the nitrogen concentration but exhibits a more moderate dependence on boron doping. At $N_B = 10^{21}$ cm$^{-3}$, varying the interface grading scale $w$ from 0.5 to 8 nm changes the depletion depth by approximately 22 nm, whereas variations in the modeled bulk BDD charge response produce a shift of only 1.27 nm. These results indicate that, under the conditions studied, the nitrogen donor concentration and local interface structure primarily govern the equilibrium NV charge-state profile, rather than the bulk electronic response of BDD alone.

How biological information changes as it crosses this architectural boundary remains poorly understood. We analyze per-residue activations from the Pairformer trunk and diffusion module of Boltz-1 using linear probes, sparse autoencoders (SAEs), and causal interventions. From the trunk, both geometry (secondary structure, disorder) and sequence chemistry (amino-acid identity, signal peptides, disulfide-bond annotations) are linearly decodable. In the diffusion module, the two diverge. Secondary structure remains equally decodable, whereas sequence chemistry becomes much less linearly accessible. We then test whether decodable directions can steer the model by editing the trunk's single representation. Helix and coil directions change predicted structure dose-dependently, but a beta-strand direction that is highly predictive on the same proteins (held-out F1 =0.78) produces no measurable increase in strand content at any of the steered layers. Removing helix or coil directions does not remove that structure. Linear decodability therefore did not imply causal influence at the sites we tested. The same probes also score markedly lower against SwissProt annotations than against DSSP labels, because unannotated residues that the model gets right are charged as false positives; such scores are therefore lower bounds. Finally, supervised probes outscore single SAE features wherever a label already exists.

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Exact Dynamic Scaling of Quantum Jump Statistics in Monitored Many-Body Systems

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (171 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.22029v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum measurement has opened a new frontier in nonequilibrium many-body physics, revealing striking phenomena such as measurement-induced entanglement transitions, whose experimental observation typically requires costly postselection. Quantum jump statistics offer another route to studying such measurement-induced many-body phenomena without postselection, motivating the search for universality in measurement outcomes themselves. In this Letter, we discover that fluctuation of the number of quantum jumps within a subsystem exhibits novel dynamic scaling, characterized by diffusive time scale and anomalous super-Poissonian system-size scaling that depend on the subsystem size in monitored many-body systems. For free fermions under continuous monitoring, we exactly determine the scaling exponent and the scaling function by deriving an exact finite-size solution of the Liouvillian autocorrelation function. We also analytically show that the dynamic scaling with the same scaling exponent and the scaling function even holds for interacting fermions in the limit of large measurement strength. Our work provides a novel framework to classify measurement-induced nonequilibrium many-body universality through experimentally friendly, postselection-free quantities.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.21992v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We develop an algorithm to propagate auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) wavefunctions in mixed precision. We target NVIDIA Tensor Cores using the TensorFloat-32 (TF32) format. We approximate each full-precision array by a TF32 leading term and a TF32 residual, and each full-precision matrix product by three TF32 products accumulated in full precision. Benchmarks on hydrogen chains show that mixed-precision propagation is consistently faster than double-precision GPU propagation, with an increasing advantage as the system size grows. The resulting local-energy deviations remain small over the propagation windows considered here. These results identify the stochastic two-body propagator as a particularly effective target for reduced precision, while our method allows higher precision to be retained for accuracy-sensitive operations. Hence, our algorithm provides a practical way to speed up AFQMC calculations and demonstrates where reduced precision can be applied without adverse effects on the method's accuracy.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Photonic Maxwells demon as an energy resource

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (198 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21972v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose a new realization of Maxwells demon for photons and its use as an energy resource. The starting point is a multilayer dielectric mirror that transmits photons within a certain wavelength band but reflects photons at longer wavelengths, followed by a material that irreversibly converts the wavelength. A 3D box constructed from these one-way mirrors is a self-acting Maxwells demon for photons. The first case considered is a one-way mirror for visible photons, converting blue to red as an example. The next case is a one-way mirror that transmits visible light but reflects infrared light, followed by a perfect blackbody. We analyze a 3D box with such mirrors as walls to accumulate and store blackbody radiation. Applications include solar-powered thermal energy and solar-powered thermophotovoltaics. The latter case would combine the 3D box with an ultra-low bandgap semiconductor photovoltaic cell inside. In the ideal optical limit, radiation can enter the box but cannot return through the entrance channel after conversion, allowing repeated photon recycling and nearly complete optical utilization. This can in principle move the conversion efficiency toward the thermodynamic limit for solar-energy conversion, the Landsberg limit of 93.3%.

Industry News: Shortest-path percolation and structural robustness of quantum internet networks

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (192 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.21855v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study shortest-path percolation on spatial networks that model the quantum internet based on optical fibers. In this process, the removal of paths describes the consumption of the entangled links used for communication. We compare finite and unrestricted path-length bounds for networks whose average degree either increases with system size or remains approximately constant. We show that networks become more robust as the average degree increases, whereas networks with approximately constant average degree exhibit a data collapse for the fixed finite bounds considered. Using Monte Carlo sampling of the shortest-path-length distribution, we estimate an equivalent path cost, a finite bound that approximately reproduces the degradation of the network in the unrestricted case. For networks with fixed average degree, this cost grows approximately as the square root of the number of nodes. Increasing the bound beyond this value requires additional computation time without appreciably changing the percolation dynamics. As a complementary result, for Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random networks, we find an empirical relation between the initial average degree and the approximately common crossing point of the percolation curves for different path-length bounds.

Industry News: Controllable Texture Tiling with Transformed RoPE-Enhanced Diffusion Models

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (247 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2606.22945v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Realistic integration of user-specified textures into scene images is a fundamental task in computer graphics and image editing. While existing material transfer and reference-guided inpainting methods can edit surface appearances, they often fail to address the specific requirements of texture tiling. This task necessitates precisely repeating a reference pattern according to user-defined parameters such as frequency, orientation, and scale. Furthermore, current generative approaches often struggle to maintain the structural fidelity of the reference texture, limited by either destructive pixel-level resampling or the lack of fine-grained spatial information in semantic image encoders, and they frequently fail to preserve the coherent lighting and geometry of the original scene. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for controllable and high-fidelity texture tiling based on Diffusion Transformers. Our approach introduces two key technical innovations to decouple spatial manipulation from content generation. First, we propose a Coordinate-Transformed Rotary Embedding mechanism. By applying 2D affine transformations directly to the relative positional embeddings between the target latent and the image condition, we achieve precise control over tiling patterns without explicit pixel warping, thereby utilizing the full information of the reference condition without degradation. Second, a Disjoint Attention Mask is employed to shield reference features from semantic leakage. This preserves structural integrity while seamlessly blending the synthesized texture with the scene's original lighting and geometry. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both control accuracy and texture fidelity.

arXiv:2512.12196v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Turning a full song into a music video (MV) requires interpreting its lyrics, which are often metaphorical, multilingual, and repeated across choruses, together with its musical character, and laying the resulting imagery out along the song's structure. Existing music-to-video systems produce short clips or audio-reactive visuals and make little use of lyric meaning. We present AutoMV, a training-free multi-agent framework in which LLM Screenwriter and Director agents plan a full-song visual narrative from time-aligned lyrics and music analysis, keep characters consistent through a shared character bank, and route each shot to cinematic or lip-sync rendering with verification. To evaluate full-song MVs, we build M2VBench: 30 released songs paired with their official MVs, objective audio--visual metrics, and a 12-criterion rubric rated by music-industry experts. Expert evaluation highlights that AutoMV outperforms other baselines, although a gap remains to human-produced MVs. Ablation studies highlight the importance of time-aligned lyrics for musical theme alignment and storytelling. We further find that the selected multimodal judge, guided by our evaluation rubric, recovers the expert ranking of automatic systems, with some discrepancies in fine-grained assessments.

Tunable Topological Charge Order in Magnetic Moir\'e Systems

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (274 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.21745v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Two-dimensional electrons in a strong magnetic field exhibit two seemingly incompatible ground states: incompressible quantum Hall liquids with a quantized Hall conductance, and electron crystals in which interactions drive the charge into ordered patterns. Moir\'e superlattices in transition-metal-dichalcogenide bilayers offer a tunable arena for this competition. Using neural quantum states (NQS) together with several methodological advances, we show how this competition unfolds. In particular, we demonstrate that the two end points are separated by an extended regime in which molecular charge order coexists with a quantized Hall response. We map the ground-state phase diagram of electrons at Landau-level filling $\nu_B=1$ in the presence of a moir\'e superlattice potential, with three electrons per moir\'e cell. In the deep triangular potential limit, the electrons form the topologically trivial "Wigner molecular crystal'' of three-electron artificial atoms, a state recently imaged at zero magnetic field in moir\'e bilayers. As the potential depth is lowered, molecular charge order remains while quantized Hall response emerges. At the honeycomb point, where each cell contains three electrons and two degenerate moir\'e minima, wells are either singly or doubly occupied and the doublons provide an emergent Ising degree of freedom. Starting from modest interaction strength, we find short-range doublon correlations within the Chern insulator which grow with interaction strength and eventually break sublattice symmetry, forming a N\'eel CDW with long-range order between doublons. The topological molecular regime lies at twist angles and magnetic fields directly accessible to current experiments. The methodological advances presented provide a scalable framework for exploring a broad range of questions in correlated quantum matter in the presence of magnetic fields.

Physics-Aware Zero-Shot Learning for Low-Dose CT from a Single Sinogram

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (217 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2504.07927v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Low-dose computed tomography (CT) imaging remains a persistent challenge, especially under heterogeneous acquisition conditions. Zero-shot learning, which enables models to learn directly from individual images without external supervision, represents a compelling approach to mitigate distribution mismatches arising from variations in scanner hardware, imaging protocols, and patient demographics. However, most existing zero-shot approaches employ down-sampling operations that reduce spatial resolution and cause domain shifts, which become particularly evident when applied to raw sinogram data. Here, we propose a physics-aware zero-shot CT denoising framework to exploit the conjugate symmetry property intrinsic to CT sinograms. Conjugate X-ray pencil beams traverse identical anatomical paths and ideally yield the same expected attenuation values but with independent noise realizations. By randomly mapping sinogram values between conjugate-ray pairs, we synthesize structurally consistent yet noise-diverse sinogram pairs, enabling self-supervised network training without external data. The resulting lightweight denoising network demonstrates strong generalization across low-dose simulation, clinical helical CT, and preclinical photon-counting CT datasets. Quantitative and qualitative results demonstrate competitive denoising performance, with favorable noise suppression and structural preservation across diverse acquisition settings. This work establishes a generalizable and data-efficient paradigm for CT denoising that integrates physical redundancy into learning-based image reconstruction. The code for the proposed method is openly available at: https://github.com/shiyongyi/Physics-Aware-Zero-Shot-CT-Sinogram-Denoising.

Representing Differential Inclusions as Monads: A Framework for Compositional Controller Synthesis

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (207 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.19469v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sequential composition of safety-certified controllers for hybrid and non-smooth robotic systems is well studied piecewise. Yet no existing framework reduces this question to a single algebraic condition. We construct a \emph{trajectory monad} for Filippov-regular differential inclusions. Its Kleisli category treats controllers as morphisms and sequential execution as trajectory concatenation. Control Barrier Function (CBF) certification, a guarantee of forward invariance, corresponds to a sub-monad of this category. Joint safety of composed controllers then follows from one algebraic condition. All controllers must land in a common sub-monad, which is closed under the monad multiplication. The sub-monad condition recasts recasts existing CBF composition practice categorically. It explains why a smooth intersection of multiple barriers supports safe composition, while enforcing barriers phase by phase does not. For the phase-by-phase case, we derive a closed-form Bernoulli model of the failure rate. We validate it over a randomized sweep of 3{,}000 instances. The same sweep reveals that the standard baseline degrades under constraint conflict as the barrier count grows. This baseline enforces all barriers simultaneously as constraints in a single quadratic program (QP). We instantiate the framework on a four-mode piecewise-affine system and on a unicycle reduced-order model over heterogeneous terrain.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (232 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2605.10931v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Transformers with self-attention modules as their core components have become an integral architecture in modern large language and foundation models. In this paper, we study the evolution of tokens in deep encoder-only transformers at inference time which is described in the large-token limit by a mean-field continuity equation. Leveraging ideas from the convergence analysis of interacting multi-particle systems, with particles corresponding to tokens, we prove that the token distribution rapidly concentrates onto the push-forward of the initial distribution under a projection map induced by the key, query, and value matrices, and remains metastable for moderate times. Specifically, we show that the Wasserstein distance of the two distributions scales like $\sqrt{{\log(\beta+1)}/{\beta}}\exp(Ct)+\exp(-ct)$ in terms of the temperature parameter $\beta^{-1}\to 0$ and inference time $t\geq 0$. For the proof, we establish Lyapunov-type estimates for the zero-temperature equation, identify its limit as $t\to\infty$, and employ a stability estimate in Wasserstein space together with a quantitative Laplace principle to couple the two equations. Our result implies that for time scales of order $\log\beta$, which correspond to the early-phase behavior most relevant for practical finite-depth models, the token distribution concentrates at the identified limiting distribution. Numerical experiments confirm this and, beyond that, complement our theory by showing that for finite $\beta$ and large $t$ the dynamics enter a different terminal phase, dominated by the spectrum of the value matrix.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.19466v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: World models learned from offline data allow an agent to plan without further interaction with the environment, but the sampling-based planners used with them handle safety constraints only by scoring or rejecting sampled action sequences. We instead pose safe planning in the latent space of a learned world model as a successive convex program (SCP), in which a learned discrete-time control barrier function is imposed as a constraint at every step of the horizon. SCP requires smooth dynamics, so we build the networks from smoothed MaxMin activations and spectrally normalised layers, and bound the resulting linearisation error in terms of the Lipschitz bound and the smoothing width. As SCP is a local method, we start it from a sampled plan. On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks with offline data, this planner has fewer violations than MPPI and CEM drawing 128 times as many samples at equal wall-clock time in our main comparison, though not significantly, and earns greater return at longer horizons, and is much safer than SCP without a sampled start. SCP converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models. Unlike sampling, it also reports at each step whether its plan is a feasible, first-order optimal KKT point of the planning problem in the model, or that no feasible plan was found nearby. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/youngers2006/scwm.

However, empirical evidence comparing quantum and classical models in realistic transfer learning settings remains limited, especially in low-data regimes. In this work, we systematically study the robustness of quantum models under reduced training data. We evaluate multiple quantum and classical architectures across diverse transfer tasks and retraining configurations, and quantify robustness using accuracy degradation and relative performance retention (RPR). Acoustic sensing, particularly using microphone arrays, could provide complementary perception capabilities for autonomous driving, but has remained largely underexplored. In this work, we design a horizontally arranged microphone array that functions as the "ears" of a vehicle, enabling localization of nearby moving vehicles in a bird's-eye view (BEV) representation that captures both their relative direction and distance. Using this array, we collect a real-world driving dataset, AcousticScenes, which contains 2,117 static and 2,863 dynamic samples with synchronized spatial acoustic signals, LiDAR point clouds and 3D bounding box annotations. Building on this dataset, we propose AcousticBEV, a learning-based method for acoustic BEV object localization, which estimates the center locations of moving traffic participants in BEV from the microphone-array signals, conditioned on the ego vehicle's own speed. Experimental results demonstrate that AcousticBEV outperforms both classical signal-processing baselines and other learning-based methods, achieving F1 scores of $47.7 \pm 1.2$% on "Easy" scenarios and $45.1 \pm 1.4$% on "Difficult" cases. Our findings demonstrate that acoustic signals from a low-cost, vehicle-mounted microphone array can localize nearby moving vehicles in both azimuth and distance.

We describe a self-contained procedure which uses finite quotients of orientation- preserving triangle groups to generate regular maps on compact genus-g surfaces. From these, one can extract their lattice connectivity, plaquette structure, homology cycles and Wilson sectors while implementing consistent boundary conditions. On the example of {8, 3} and {12, 3} lattices, we enumerate a selection of quotients with up to 72 vertices, which constitute the discrete steps in a finite-size scaling analysis. We then discuss how the resulting ground state sector degeneracies are entirely generated by physical lattice symmetries acting on both the plaquette fluxes and non-contractible Wilson loops. Finally, we study the behaviour of the finite-size two-vison gap and matter fermion correlations. We find that the gap does not decrease monotonically with increasing system size, while one still recovers the expected algebraic decay of the correlations at the isotropic point, even for the considered modest system sizes.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.19272v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper shapes a swarm into a target pattern, such as a figure taken from an image, by controlling its spatial moments. The image is sampled into a reference configuration whose centroid and covariance set the position and principal spreads of the formation, while its higher-order moments, expressed in covariance-normalized (whitened) coordinates, encode the remaining shape. In contrast with geometric formation control, which prescribes distances, bearings, or relative positions between specific agents, this specification concerns the swarm as a whole and assigns no agent to a particular place. The key mechanism is orthogonalization in the swarm's own empirical inner product: projecting negative-gradient velocities onto the complement of low-degree polynomials sampled at the agents makes every higher-order correction preserve all lower-order moments exactly. The resulting hierarchical controller has lower triangular error dynamics and converges locally exponentially for any positive gains, so orders can be added without undoing those already achieved. A joint alternative regulates the higher moments together through a regularized Gauss--Newton step while preserving the centroid and covariance dynamics. We give bounds on the number of agents and sufficient conditions for regularity. Both controllers admit a distributed implementation that uses only relative positions and neighbor communication and retains local exponential convergence when estimation is sufficiently fast. In a distributed simulation on a sparse graph, 350 agents form an airplane from an unstructured swarm through moments up to order ten; the hierarchy reaches the full specification, while the joint law approaches it with smaller velocities.

While KKL observers offer a rigorous theoretical framework by immersing nonlinear dynamics into a stable linear latent space, its practical realization relies on solving Partial Differential Equations (PDE) that are analytically intractable. In a recent development, arXiv:2511.18820v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We present a physics-constrained neural solver for incompressible flow that requires neither labeled data nor supervised pretraining. The solver enforces incompressibility and boundary conditions (BCs) to strict tolerances. We attribute the limited Reynolds numbers of existing physics-informed approaches to insufficient enforcement of these constraints, on which conventional finite-difference and finite-volume solvers depend. We therefore formulate incompressible flow as a constrained optimization problem within the physics- and equality-constrained artificial neural network (PECANN) framework: the pressure Poisson residual is minimized subject to the momentum equations, continuity equation, and BCs imposed as equality constraints on the primitive variables, while a conditionally adaptive augmented Lagrangian method enforces each constraint. The pressure Poisson objective proves critical. Across all benchmarks, replacing it with the momentum residual fails to converge to accurate solutions under identical architecture and constraint enforcement, which we attribute to the global elliptic coupling of pressure and velocity that local momentum-residual minimization lacks. For advection-dominated flows, we introduce an adaptive vanishing entropy viscosity that stabilizes training while leaving the converged solution unchanged. The solver predicts lid-driven cavity flow up to Re = 7,500 with centerline velocity profiles matching benchmark data, and is further validated on flow over a backward-facing step at Re = 800, 3D unsteady Beltrami flow, and steady and unsteady flow past a circular cylinder under an inflow-outflow configuration, for which an ablation study identifies admissible outlet BCs for velocity and pressure. From a randomly initialized network and without external perturbations, the solver captures the spontaneous onset of periodic vortex shedding in unsteady cylinder flow.

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.19088v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability computes the maximal safe set and a safety filter for a given obstacle configuration, but it must be re-solved whenever the obstacles change, which a deployed robot cannot afford. Learning a single value function conditioned on the obstacle set removes the re-solve, yet it sharpens the central weakness of learned reachability: one network must now cover a whole family of safety problems, and its approximation error carries no preferred sign, so rare obstacle configurations silently produce false-safe states. To address these challenges, we present a conditioned reachability model designed so that the remaining error falls on the conservative side. Specifically, our method caps the obstacle margin, which makes the value function provably local, in the sense that obstacles farther than a known threshold cannot affect it, so the model reads only a body-frame window, trains on small scenes, and transfers to scenes of any size with millisecond per-scene preparation. Moreover, the output structure builds the value bound into the model. By training with counterexample mining over the finite-dimensional window configuration space, we maximize the claimed safe volume subject to the HJ inequality, so the learned set grows toward the true safe set from the conservative side. Across all tested obstacle settings, ours is the only method that combines recovery comparable to per-scene DeepReach training with near-zero rollout collisions. We also extend the method to a 10D quadrotor, again with markedly lower collision rates than the baselines.

It has been revealed that arXiv:2611.21054v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Dataset distillation (DD) replaces large training datasets with smaller synthetic ones to reduce computational costs. While traditionally used for classification, we present, to our knowledge, the first DD study for line-level handwritten text recognition (HTR). Unlike classification tasks, which use discrete labels, HTR employs unaligned sequences from a virtually infinite output space as labels. To adapt classification-based DD methods to this scenario, we define text pseudo-classes by clustering transcriptions based on character n-grams. We adapt gradient matching (GM), distribution matching (DM) and trajectory matching (MTT) to a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN) trained with Connectionist Temporal Classification (CTC). In this process, synthetic line images are generated by optimising only the pixels of real starting lines (either randomly chosen or selected as text medoids), while keeping their original transcriptions fixed. Across four datasets (IAM, George Washington, READ\,2016, LAM) and three budgets (1--10\,\% of the training lines), no distilled set outperforms its real initialisation lines. Random lines prove better than medoids, and further optimisation only degrades recognition. Methodologically, DM lowers its objective without benefit, while GM and MTT barely move theirs. We turn these findings into guidelines for evaluating data compression in HTR.

Existing acceleration methods reduce parts of this overhead, while historical KV reading and cache construction remain costly across video chunks. To address these challenges, we propose ScoutCache, a training-free framework that jointly optimizes denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction. We observe that shallow feature changes provide useful information for estimating clean latent updates, while historical KV dependence varies across Transformer layers and attention heads but remains relatively stable across video chunks. Based on these observations, we develop Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. We further introduce Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical reading budgets based on attention output perturbations, and Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to reduce cache construction costs by selecting informative spatial tokens while maintaining spatial coverage. Extensive experiments on Self-Forcing and LongLive using VBench and MovieGen demonstrate that ScoutCache achieves up to 2.28$\times$ and 1.86$\times$ speedups, respectively, while consistently improving generation quality without modifying pretrained model parameters.

FAVR: Flow-Aware Visual Residual Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Policies

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (192 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.20971v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pretrained video representations provide rich temporal information for robotic manipulation, yet effectively integrating them into existing vision-language-action (VLA) policies remains challenging. We present Flow-Aware Visual Residual Alignment (FAVR), a lightweight framework for flow-aware visual conditioning of frozen VLA policies. FAVR maintains a compact temporal visual state through linear Test-Time Training (TTT) and retrieves action-conditioned visual features throughout flow-based action generation. By exploiting the affine structure of the frozen action head, we explicitly characterize how injected visual features influence predicted action velocities and formulate flow-aware channel selection as a box-constrained optimization problem. We develop a FISTA-based solver for joint gate optimization and derive an efficient closed-form approximation through diagonalization and rescaling. With only 1.74-2.19M trainable parameters and 5,000 adaptation steps, FAVR improves pretrained VLA policies across benchmarks. On RoboTwin 2.0, FAVR improves LingBot-VLA from 87.12% to 90.04% under clean conditions and from 86.88% to 89.38% under randomized conditions. A controlled ablation on five RoboTwin tasks further demonstrates that flow-aware gating increases average success from 72.0% with a gate shared across flow steps to 82.0%, demonstrating the benefit of adapting visual conditioning throughout action generation.
